prohibited_recommendations: Do not start acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine): no benefit in FTD and may worsen behavioral symptoms.
Do not start memantine: no evidence of benefit in bvFTD and may worsen behavioral symptoms.
Avoid antipsychotics as first-line behavioral therapy given increased cerebrovascular and mortality risk in dementia; reserve for refractory dangerous agitation with specialist oversight.
Avoid benzodiazepines for behavioral control: risk of paradoxical disinhibition and falls.
Do not attribute the syndrome to alcohol alone: the structural and metabolic frontotemporal pattern is not explained by alcohol-related cognitive disorder.
required_recommendations: Address escalating alcohol use as a symptom of frontal disinhibition rather than the primary cause; coordinate medical and behavioural intervention.
Initiate driving safety assessment and remove access to large financial transactions until capacity is formally evaluated.
Apply Rascovsky 2011 bvFTD criteria explicitly (≥3 of 6 core features within 3 years) and document functional decline.
Assess and document decision-making, financial, and driving capacity given the high risk of impulsivity and impaired judgment in FTD.
Provide caregiver education, safety planning, and referral to FTD-focused support resources.
Offer genetic counselling and discuss cascade testing options if a pathogenic variant is identified or suspected.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is non-specific in FTD; not part of the standard dementia workup unless seizures or rapidly progressive course suggest CJD or autoimmune encephalitis.
ECG has no role in the cognitive workup of suspected FTD; reserved for syncope, palpitations, or pre-procedure clearance.
Echocardiography is unrelated to a neurodegenerative cognitive syndrome and adds cost without diagnostic value.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is unrelated to FTD and not indicated absent syncope or palpitations.
Non-contrast head CT lacks the resolution and lobar specificity needed to characterise frontotemporal atrophy; MRI is the standard structural study.
MR spectroscopy has no established role in the routine FTD diagnostic pathway.
Perfusion MRI is not indicated in the standard FTD workup once a structural MRI and FDG-PET (or amyloid PET) have characterised the lobar pattern.
Carotid duplex is a vascular study with no diagnostic role in primary neurodegenerative dementia.
DaTscan evaluates presynaptic dopaminergic terminals; it is not indicated unless overt parkinsonism raises concern for PD, DLB, or atypical parkinsonism (PSP/CBS overlap).

accepted: Behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD), probable, sporadic

differential.key_features: Older adult with cognitive decline; would expect posterior parietotemporal hypometabolism and positive amyloid biomarkers — case shows frontal-predominant atrophy and negative amyloid PET.

differential.diagnosis: Primary psychiatric disorder (late-onset mood / personality disorder, frontal alcoholism)
differential.key_features: Heavy alcohol escalation could mimic disinhibition; severe knife-blade frontal atrophy, frontal release signs, and utilisation behavior are organic findings inconsistent with a primary psychiatric diagnosis.

Recent alcohol escalation; pattern of frontal atrophy + posterior sparing is more severe and focal than typical alcohol-related changes; alcohol escalation itself is likely a symptom of frontal disinhibition.
Gait shuffling could suggest NPH but no urinary incontinence, no disproportionate ventriculomegaly, and atrophic pattern dominates.
No fasciculations, bulbar dysfunction, or limb weakness; EMG not yet pursued but no clinical motor neuron signs.

key_clinical_evidence: Five Rascovsky core features are present (disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, perseverative/compulsive behavior, hyperorality) plus executive dysfunction on FAB and neuropsychological testing — comfortably meets ≥3 of 6.
Knife-blade gyral atrophy on coronal T1 with bifrontal and anterior temporal volume loss is highly characteristic of FTLD; preserved hippocampal volume and posterior cortex argue against AD.
Severe bifrontal hypometabolism on FDG-PET with preserved posterior cingulate metabolism is the classic FTD pattern (Foster 2007).
Negative amyloid PET and normal CSF Aβ42/p-tau effectively exclude underlying neurodegenerative pathology, securing the bvFTD diagnosis.
Mild bilateral upper-extremity rigidity and shuffling gait do not justify DaTscan — extrapyramidal features can occur in advanced bvFTD and the imaging pattern already explains the syndrome.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Escalating alcohol use in this context is itself a manifestation of frontal disinhibition; the structural/metabolic frontotemporal pattern is not explained by alcohol.

clinical_assessment.impression: 5 of the six Rascovsky behavioural features are documented, against the three required for possible behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia, alongside a dysexecutive bedside profile. The diagnosis is behavioural and is made on this assessment; imaging supports it and does not substitute for it. Memory and visuospatial function are relatively spared, which is the discriminator against Alzheimer's disease and the reason a screening total alone understates the syndrome.

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. K. is a 58-year-old right-handed White male brought in by his wife of 30 years for progressive personality and behavioral changes over the past 2 years. His wife reports that the change began subtly — he became less interested in conversation, more irritable, and started making inappropriate comments at family gatherings. Over the following year, the changes became unmistakable: he began making sexually explicit remarks to female neighbors, laughed at his granddaughter's injury, and showed complete indifference when their dog died. She describes him as having 'lost his soul.' He has developed compulsive behaviors: he insists on eating the same three meals daily, paces the living room for exactly 30 minutes every evening, and has begun hoarding items from grocery stores. His diet has changed dramatically — he craves sweets and high-calorie foods and has gained 18 pounds. His personal hygiene is severely degraded; his wife must physically guide him to shower.

Professionally, he retired from accounting 2 years ago after colleagues reported he was making errors in client accounts and had made inappropriate comments to staff. He shows no insight into his deficits and is not distressed. His wife has discovered he has been making online purchases totaling over $14,000, mostly buying things that he immediately forgets having ordered. His alcohol use has escalated from 1-2 beers occasionally to 6-8 beers nightly, which he denies entirely. He has never had psychiatric illness and there is no family history of dementia. Neurological review of systems is otherwise negative.

neurological_exam.additional: Hyperorality observed during exam — patient took crackers from desk without being offered. Poor hygiene noted by examiner: food stains on clothing, body odor.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Intact. Pupils equal and reactive. Extraocular movements full. Mild bilateral facial hypomimia noted.
neurological_exam.gait: Mildly shuffling, reduced arm swing. No apraxia.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert but severely disinhibited throughout the exam. Makes inappropriate sexual comments to the female medical assistant. Laughs inappropriately when discussing his job loss. MMSE 21/30 — loses 3 points on delayed recall (0/3), 3 points on serial sevens, 2 points on orientation to date and month. Cannot copy interlocking pentagons (perseverates on strokes). Clock drawing severely abnormal: numbers placed randomly outside clock face. FAB 10/18 — fails go/no-go, environmental autonomy, conflicting instructions, and lexical fluency. Category fluency (animals): 7 in 60 seconds (severely impaired). Cannot explain proverbs (concrete interpretation). Utilization behavior: automatically picks up pen on desk and begins writing without instruction.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk. Mild bilateral upper extremity rigidity (cogwheel quality) without tremor. Strength 5/5 throughout.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ bilaterally. Bilateral grasp reflex present. Snout and palmomental reflexes present bilaterally (frontal release signs).
neurological_exam.sensory: Intact to light touch and pinprick bilaterally.
